book.title: The Design of Everyday Things
book.author: Don Norman
book.description: One of the world's great designers shares his vision of "the fundamental principles of great and meaningful design", that's "even more relevant today than it was when first published" (Tim Brown, CEO, IDEO). Even the smartest among us can feel inept as we fail to figure out which light switch or oven burner to turn on, or whether to push, pull, or slide a door. The fault, argues this ingenious -- even liberating -- book, lies not in ourselves, but in product design that ignores the needs of users and the principles of cognitive psychology. The problems range from ambiguous and hidden controls to arbitrary relationships between controls and functions, coupled with a lack of feedback or other assistance and unreasonable demands on memorization. The Design of Everyday Things shows that good, usable design is possible. The rules are simple: make things visible, exploit natural relationships that couple function and control, and make intelligent use of constraints. The goal: guide the user effortlessly to the right action on the right control at the right time. The Design of Everyday Things is a powerful primer on how -- and why -- some products satisfy customers while others only frustrate them.

note.text: Which things should be paid attention to, which should be ignored? Industry faces this problem all the time, as do governments. The intelligence communities are swamped with data — how do they decide which cases are serious?

The author appears to think of design as something deeply important for decision-making in a complex context. This problem is very prevalent and dominant today in the promises of AI. AI will consume a lot of information, but to distinguish which one is serious, which one is crucial, and which one is not is very difficult, given that everything is just words to LLMs. It's interesting and surprising that the author even mentioned artificial intelligence here.

A more powerful approach is to develop intelligent computer systems, using good search and appropriate reasoning techniques — artificial intelligence — decision-making and problem-solving. The difficulties here are in establishing the interaction of the people with automation. Human teams and automated systems have to be thought of as collaborative, cooperative systems.

This usually means that machines do the parts that are easy for people, but when the problems become complex — which is precisely when people could use assistance — that is when the machines usually fail.

He tries to foresee the future a bit, but it's not very accurate now. He discusses this in the context of "the design of future things." This is super interesting because AI has advanced a lot compared to when the book was published. Artificial intelligence actually helps me in a lot of complex contexts — it helps me to better understand, better dive in, better gather touch points, etc. Still, it is very bad at making decisions. Maybe it's worth it to skim "The Design of Future Things."

note.text: The author listed down the seven stages of action. It's a bit of a repeat from the beginning of the chapter, but it's quite useful. There are seven stages of action and seven fundamental design principles. It's nice to see that we capture the seven actions as seven questions that people ask themselves when performing actions.

1. What do I want to accomplish? 2. What are the alternative action sequences? 3. What action can I do now? 4. How do I do it? 5. What happened? 6. What does it mean? 7. Is it okay? Have I accomplished my goal?

These are the seven questions that people ask themselves when they walk through a course of action. Together with them, there are seven fundamental design principles. The trap here is that I find it a bit misleading because the seven principles do not map to the seven stages of action. They are orthogonal to them. It's a bit misleading in terms of conceptual model — it's not a good mapping, if I use the terms of the very author themselves.
The seven principles are: discoverability, feedback, conceptual model, affordances, signifiers, mappings, and constraints.

note.text: Conceptual models are a form of story resulting from our predisposition to find explanations. These models are essential in helping us understand our experiences, predict the outcome of actions, and handle unexpected occurrences. We base our models on whatever knowledge we have, real or imaginary, naive or sophisticated.

This is interesting because I care about storytelling and I care about conceptual models, but this is the first time I've heard someone say that conceptual models, like mental models, are a kind of storytelling — connecting the power of concepts and the power of storytelling.

note.text: This section is about the three layers of processing that people have. The first is visceral — it's immediate, like a reflex when people do things. The second is behavioral — when we do certain tasks repeatedly, they become behavioral. The third is reflective — people reflect, think about things, and decide whether they like something or not.
Usually when we plan, it is reflective; when we specify, it is behavioral; and when we perform, it is mostly visceral.
In the scope that I work in though — ads, experimentation — I think most of the time people operate at the reflective layer.

note.text: The book takes a lot of sidetracks, which makes the information not very dense. Most of the sidetracks I don't like that much. There is one sidetrack that is interesting though — when the author talks about how positive and negative emotional states affect how people operate.

A positive emotional state is ideal for creative thought, but it is not very well suited for getting things done. Too much, and we call the person scatterbrained, flitting from one topic to another, unable to finish one thought before another comes to mind. A brain in a negative emotional state provides focus, precisely what is needed to maintain attention on a task and finish it. Too much, however, and we get tunnel vision, when people are unable to look beyond their narrow point of view. Both the positive, relaxed state and the anxious, negative, intense state are valuable and powerful tools for human creativity and action. The extremes of both states, however, can be dangerous.

I never thought of it this way. When you are positive, happy, and optimistic, you are more creative — but execution needs a certain dose of stress and anxiety. This is a good balance to look at. An interesting sidetrack, but I still don't like when books go off track too much and the information gets less dense.

note.text: Chapter 2 is about the psychology of everyday things. It introduces some interesting concepts.
First, there is the gulf of execution: What can I do? What should I do now? How do I do it? That's the gulf of execution.
Then there is the gulf of evaluation, which is about feedback: What have I done? Was it good? What do I expect now?
Good design should help people overcome these gulfs.

The book then breaks down the gulfs further into the seven stages of action: setting up the goal, then plan, specify, perform, perceive, interpret, and compare. That's how people interact with the world.
So far the book is mostly interesting up to this point.

note.text: Another interesting concept is what the author calls conceptual models, or more generally what people call mental models. Usually mental models can be conveyed through the design but can also live in people's heads, and the designers and the end users usually have different conceptual models, different mental models. For the design to convey a good, accurate, useful conceptual model to the end user is crucial — it's one of the key goals of having good design.
